title: The Neverending Story- Extended Gmork scene

commenti.body:
Interesting. But I think I’d want to see the international version. Are you saying that In it— there is a rumble and earthquake which throws a dagger-shaped rock to the floor, Atreyu picks it up, (no dialogue), Gmork attacks? 

If I understand correctly, my read would be:

The international version is subtler, I think. In it, the moment of recognition — which includes the question of who realizes the other is the other first, who attacks who first — are left entirely to interpretation. 

I suppose it is possible in the international version that Gmork doesn’t know its Atreyu even up to the moment of its death, and that it only attacks Atreyu because Atreyu picks up the knife. Of course, Gmork announces early on he will be its last victim no matter. So Atreyu is justified in picking up the knife no matter. Two strangers on the road.

Only, I don’t think that makes any sense… even in the international version. Even if only that it carries no meaning. Fantasia is a hero story, it is a world of the hero story, and this encounter has to be meaningful. It’s the crux of the story within the story. The international version needs to bring us to the point of mutual recognition where the hero faces his arch enemy and has a final battle. To get to that point without the final dialogue, we assume that Gmork is being sly, maybe he surmises it’s Atreyu at some point, maybe they both recognize each other at the same time. It’s hard to see if this interpretation holds up without seeing that version. I’d expect to look for moments of recognition, or moments where it seems like Gmork is lying, merely pretending not to recognize Atreyu. 

You can understand why one would make the exchange more obvious and/or more obvious for an American audience that is less appreciative of subtlety. In it, Atreyu, upon understanding what Gmork is, immediately recognizes what he must do, announces himself, and does it. Gmork reacts appropriately. Nothing is subtle, but I think we still wind up at the same place.

Not for nothing—I suppose the dialogue paints Atreyu as more of the badass that he actually is. He acts immediately, from instinct, without reflection on his options or his death. He takes a stand. He announces his name. He is an unflinching badass. (Not unimportantly, Gmork also embraces its identity in the face of its own death, adding to the tragic irony. Atreyu and Gmork are indomitable and opposing forces.)

For this final reason—that it gives voices to Atreyu’s triumph—the edit makes the film stronger but probably not so different.

Atreyu tells him who he is in both versions. The interntional version cuts out Gmork saying he’s weak and Atreyu saying he’ll “give him” strength. In the international version Atreyu grabs the stone and orders Gmork to fight as soon as he realizes Gmork is after hI’m.
